title: Al-An'am
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Al-An'am, "The Cattle," is a Makkan surah of one hundred and sixty-five verses. It opens with praise of Allah for creating the heavens and the earth and making darkness and light, and its subject throughout is the oneness of Allah: who He is, what He has made, and why setting up partners beside Him is folly.

### Where and when it was revealed

There is no disagreement that the whole of Al-An'am was revealed in Makkah. Ibn 'Abbas said so, in the report of 'Ikrimah and 'Ata' from him, and 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr said the same, in the report of Khasif from Mujahid. The leading scholars of tafsir agree. Ibn 'Abbas added, in a report recorded by At-Tabarani, that all of it was revealed at night, accompanied by seventy thousand angels raising their voices in glorification of Allah. As-Suddi said that Murrah said that 'Abdullah said it was revealed in the company of seventy thousand angels. Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Qatadah said more or less the same: the whole surah came down at one time, except for a few verses.

### What the surah covers

The surah begins by praising Allah as Creator of the heavens and the earth and Maker of darkness and light, then turns to the disbelievers who set up equals to their Lord. It argues that the Being who created everything cannot need a partner, and it answers the many false notions of its day. The Magians (Majus) made light and darkness into two creators, Yazdan and Ahriman. The polytheists of Arabia worshipped stones and trees. The Arya Samajists took spirit and matter to be pre-existent and independent. The Christians, despite professing one God, took 'Isa (Jesus) and his blessed mother as partners and relied on the theory of Unity in Trinity. The surah refutes all of these by saying that Allah is the sole Creator and Maker of everything, so ascribing partners to His divinity makes no sense.

The heavens are mentioned in the plural and the earth in the singular. One reading, in al-Bahr al-Muhit, takes this to mean that the seven heavens differ from one another in form and attributes while the seven earths are alike, so they are counted as one. This is tied to the verse that says the earth is seven like the heavens (65:12). Darkness is named in the plural and light in the singular, because An-Nur, the light, is more honored: it stands for the one straight path, while the many darknesses stand for the many paths of error. Creation is expressed as "created" for the heavens and the earth but "made" for darkness and light, to show that darkness and light are not independent and self-existent things but contingents and attributes. Darkness is named first because it is basic to this world, light coming only where particulars are present.

The surah also sets out the terms appointed for human life: a term for death and another, known only to Allah, for the Hereafter. It reminds the reader that Allah knows what is concealed and what is revealed and what people earn. It speaks of Adam, created from clay, and of the nations who received scripture before and denied it. It warns those who take Allah's signs lightly, and it consoles the Prophet ﷺ with the pattern of prophetic rejection. It speaks of sleep and death as signs of Allah's power over souls, of how all turn to Allah alone in crisis, and of the gradual destruction of defiant nations. It tells the story of Ibrahim (Abraham) rejecting his father's idolatry and arguing from the observation of creation. It names the ten divine commandments, refutes those who deny revelation, and sets out what is lawful and unlawful to eat, including the rules about cattle. It closes with the gathering of jinn and humans on the Day of Judgment and the complete dedication of life to Allah.

Along the way it cites other verses to make its points: the heavens and the earth in (16:48) and (65:12), the straight path in (6:153), the taking of souls by night in (6:60), the knowledge of the Hour in (7:187) and (79:42-44), and Allah as God of heaven and earth in (43:84).

### Its virtues

Al-Asfra'ini said that this surah consists of all the principles and subsidiaries of tawhid (oneness of Allah). It was prefaced with "Al-Hamdulillah" to teach that all praise belongs to Allah, who needs no praise from anyone, and the creation of the heavens and the earth and of darkness and light is the proof of His being the Praised One. The system by which heaven and earth are governed is so perfect in its coordination and unitary nature that it proclaims aloud that its Creator and Organiser can be none other than the one and only God. The flawlessly regulated revolution of the earth and the coming of light and darkness and day and night are events beyond human comprehension, and they show that God does not need any assistant in His creation or in His control of what He has created.

### In short

- Al-An'am is a Makkan surah of one hundred and sixty-five verses about the oneness of Allah.
- It was revealed in Makkah, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others, all at one time and at night with seventy thousand angels.
- It argues from creation that Allah alone deserves worship, and answers the false beliefs of its day.
- It sets out the terms of human life and death, the laws of lawful and unlawful food, and the gathering of all on the Day of Judgment.
- Al-Asfra'ini called it a summary of all the principles and subsidiaries of tawhid.
